title: Word Counter
description: Word Counter helps people count working text copied from documents, forms, spreadsheets, email, or a CMS and review the result before using it in another system.
intro: Word Counter is for a concrete handoff: take working text copied from documents, forms, spreadsheets, email, or a CMS from a real task, produce the form the next editor, API, document, or workflow expects, and keep enough context to verify what changed.
audience: Writers, editors, marketers, students, operations teams, and developers cleaning copied text
input: The actual paragraph, list, title, or draft that needs word counter, including the problem area.
outcome: A word counter result that preserves the intended meaning and is ready to test in its destination.
review: Read the changed section in context and confirm intentional punctuation, spacing, capitalization, repetition, and paragraph boundaries remain correct.
bestFor: Small and medium working text copied from documents, forms, spreadsheets, email, or a CMS samples used for debugging, documentation, migration preparation, review, and reproducible tests.
steps: Paste a representative text sample from the task you are working on.
Run Word Counter and compare the first meaningful change with the source.
Inspect words, punctuation, spacing, and intentional structure.
Copy or download the result, then validate it in the editor, runtime, API, form, or publishing system where it will be used.
useCases: Word Counter for a real editing or publishing task rather than a synthetic keyword example.
Preparing Word Counter input and output for a bug report, documentation page, test fixture, or technical handoff.
Using Word Counter to compare the source and result before a migration, import, release, or review.
Word Counter helps catch structural or meaning-changing mistakes before the output reaches another system.

tips: Keep the original Word Counter input beside the result until the destination check passes.
Use realistic working text copied from documents, forms, spreadsheets, email, or a CMS instead of a one-word sample when validating Word Counter.
Do not assume the visual cleanup from Word Counter proves that working text copied from documents, forms, spreadsheets, email, or a CMS is valid.
Run the normal project, API, schema, browser, or editorial validation after using Word Counter.

faq.question: Who uses Word Counter?
faq.answer: Writers, editors, marketers, students, operations teams, and developers cleaning copied text use Word Counter when they need to count working text copied from documents, forms, spreadsheets, email, or a CMS before continuing work in another editor, system, or document.

faq.question: What should I paste into Word Counter?
faq.answer: Paste a focused but representative sample of working text copied from documents, forms, spreadsheets, email, or a CMS into Word Counter. Include the nesting, punctuation, characters, or edge cases that affect the real task.

faq.question: What does Word Counter change?
faq.answer: Word Counter changes the representation needed for this task. Compare the output with the source to confirm that values and intended meaning remain correct.

faq.question: What should I check after using Word Counter?
faq.answer: After Word Counter, review punctuation, spacing, capitalization, intentional repetition, paragraph boundaries, and any publishing length limit.

faq.question: Can I use the Word Counter output in production?
faq.answer: Use the Word Counter result as reviewed working output, then run the destination system's normal validation, tests, schema checks, or editorial review before production use.

faq.question: Does Word Counter store my input?
faq.answer: Word Counter has no account or saved-history feature. Even so, remove passwords, private keys, session cookies, personal data, and production secrets before using any online tool.

keywords: count working text copied from documents, forms, spreadsheets, email, or a cms
commonMistakes: Running Word Counter with a sample that does not represent the real input.
Using the Word Counter result without comparing it with the original source.
Skipping validation in the editor, runtime, API, or document that receives the output.
